code.title: A blocked thread delays timers

followUps:
Four kinds of work go to the libuv thread pool: file system calls (fs.* except the sync ones and watchers), dns.lookup, some crypto (pbkdf2, scrypt, randomBytes) and zlib compression.

Network sockets, pipes and timers do not use it; the kernel notifies the loop directly. With the default 4 threads, 10 simultaneous pbkdf2 calls run in rounds of 4, 4 and 2.

Use worker_threads for CPU work, or cluster / several processes to use more cores for a server. Each worker gets its own V8 isolate, call stack and event loop, so JavaScript really runs in parallel.

Example: on an 8-core machine, split a 1,000,000-item job into 8 chunks of 125,000 and send each to a worker. The cost is message passing and start-up time (tens of milliseconds), so reuse workers from a pool.

code.title: Event loop phase order inside an I/O callback

followUps:
It blocks in the poll phase, waiting for I/O to become ready, but only when there is nothing else to do. Node asks the OS to wait (epoll, kqueue or IOCP) with a timeout equal to the time until the next timer.

If a timer is due in 30 ms and no I/O arrives, the thread sleeps about 30 ms and then wakes for the timers phase. If a setImmediate is pending, the timeout is 0 and the loop does not sleep at all.

Active, referenced handles and pending requests keep it alive: open servers, sockets, intervals and timers, child processes, file watchers and in-flight fs or DNS requests.

When the count drops to zero the loop exits. A one-shot setTimeout(fn, 5000) keeps Node running for 5 seconds; call unref() on it and the process exits immediately. process.getActiveResourcesInfo() lists what is holding it.

Because the loop start-up time and the clock decide which comes first. setTimeout(0) really means at least 1 ms, and whether 1 ms has passed when the loop first reaches the timers phase depends on how busy the machine is.

So at top level the order can be timeout then immediate, or the reverse, from run to run. Inside an I/O callback the order is fixed: setImmediate always runs first, because the check phase follows poll.

code.title: nextTick, microtasks and setImmediate order

followUps:
Yes: a function that schedules itself with process.nextTick never lets the loop reach the next phase, so timers and I/O wait forever.

function spin() { process.nextTick(spin); }
spin();
setTimeout(() => console.log('never printed'), 10);

The tick queue is drained completely after each operation, and each run adds another entry, so the queue is never empty. Replace nextTick with setImmediate and the timer fires, because each immediate yields to the loop.

Because queueMicrotask is the standard, portable way to run something after the current code, and nextTick has a Node-only quirk: it jumps ahead of promises and can starve I/O.

Both run before any I/O, but ordering between nextTick and promises differs between CommonJS (tick first) and ES module top level (promises first). Code that uses queueMicrotask behaves the same in browsers and Node, so it is easier to reason about.

code.title: Thread pool saturation model

followUps:
More threads do not add CPU cores: 256 threads on 4 cores just fight for time, and each thread costs memory (about 1 MB of stack reserved) plus context-switch overhead. The hard maximum is 1024 in libuv.

Hashing is CPU-bound, so a pool near the core count (say 8 on an 8-core box) is best. A huge pool lets 256 bcrypt jobs all run at once, each taking 32 times longer, so every login gets slower and latency becomes less predictable.

Measure the thread-pool queue directly and show that fs and DNS latency rises exactly when the hashes run. Then change one thing and see the effect.

  1. Time a cheap fs.stat (or dns.lookup) every 100 ms and log its latency next to the event-loop delay.
  2. Run a burst of 20 bcrypt.hash calls: fs latency jumps from about 1 ms to hundreds of ms while loop delay stays low.
  3. Set UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=8 and repeat; latency should shrink.

code.title: Backpressure with write() and drain

followUps:
For byte streams the default highWaterMark is 64 KiB in current Node (it was 16 KiB before Node 22); for file read streams it was already 64 KiB.

It is a threshold, not a hard limit: write() returns false once the buffered size reaches it, but the data is still accepted. Check stream.writableHighWaterMark on your own runtime, because the default changed between versions.

In object mode highWaterMark counts objects, not bytes, and the default is 16 objects. A writable buffering 16 objects of any size will signal backpressure.

This means size is ignored: 16 small ids and 16 objects of 5 MB each both reach the limit. If objects are large, set a smaller number such as 2 or 4, so you do not hold 80 MB of them in memory before the producer is told to pause.

code.title: pipe() vs pipeline() error handling

followUps:
Pass an AbortSignal to pipeline; when you call controller.abort() every stream is destroyed and the callback or promise gets an AbortError.

const ac = new AbortController();
setTimeout(() => ac.abort(), 5000);
await pipeline(src, gzip, dst, { signal: ac.signal });

This is the standard way to add a timeout to a copy. You can also destroy any one stream with an error, and pipeline tears down the rest.

stream.finished() tells you when one stream is done, either finished normally or failed, and calls back once. It is useful when you manage streams by hand.

It fires for end, finish, error and premature close (for example a client disconnecting mid-response). For a single stream, finished(res, cb) is safer than listening to 'end' and 'error' separately, because it covers all the ways a stream can stop.

code.title: A small EventEmitter with once and off

followUps:
Synchronous emit is the contract: when emit() returns, every listener has run. That makes order predictable and lets the emitter use return values, like the boolean for "had listeners".

It also means a slow listener delays the emitter, and a thrown error propagates to the caller of emit. If you need async delivery, listeners can defer their own work with setImmediate or queueMicrotask. Emitting inside a constructor is a trap: no one can attach listeners yet, so defer with nextTick.

events.once(emitter, 'x') returns a promise that resolves with the argument array when the event fires, and rejects if 'error' is emitted first.

try {
  const [data] = await once(socket, 'ready');
} catch (err) { /* 'error' event */ }

When it settles it removes its listeners, so there is no leak. If you wait on the 'error' event itself, it resolves instead of rejecting. Pass a signal option to cancel the wait.

code.title: worker_threads with SharedArrayBuffer

followUps:
A worker shares the process (same PID, same OS memory space) but not JavaScript state: each worker has its own V8 heap, globals and event loop. Data is copied with postMessage (structured clone) unless you transfer or share it.

Shareable things: SharedArrayBuffer (use Atomics to avoid races), transferred ArrayBuffers (moved, the sender loses them), and process.env copies. Objects, closures and module variables are never shared.

Have the primary listen for 'exit' and fork a replacement, with a limit on restart rate, and drain the old worker instead of killing it where possible.

  1. On SIGTERM the worker stops accepting (server.close()), finishes in-flight requests, then exits.
  2. The primary on 'exit' forks a new worker unless it is shutting down.
  3. Add backoff, for example at most 5 restarts per minute, so a crash loop does not spin the CPU.

code.title: Module cache and circular require

followUps:
Delete its entry from require.cache and require it again; the file is then read and executed afresh.

const id = require.resolve('./config');
delete require.cache[id];
const cfg = require('./config');

Caveats: anyone who already holds the old exports keeps the old object, modules that required it stay cached, and open resources are not closed. Hot reload tools restart the process instead. ESM has no cache you can delete; a query string on the specifier (import('./a.mjs?v=2')) creates a new instance but leaks the old one.

ESM cycles work through live bindings, so a cycle partner sees the value once it is assigned, not a frozen copy. But reading a let, const or class binding before its module has run throws a ReferenceError (temporal dead zone).

Function declarations are hoisted and safe to call early. So in CJS you see undefined for a missing property, while in ESM you may see an error, but a later read gives the right value without any workaround.

code.title: Live bindings vs copied values

followUps:
It is when one package gets loaded twice, once as CJS and once as ESM, giving two separate copies with separate state.

Example: a library keeps a singleton cache. An app imports it with import, a plugin loads it with require, and now there are two caches and instanceof checks fail between them. Fixes: ship ESM only, make the CJS entry a thin wrapper that re-exports the ESM build, or keep state in a separate file used by both.

Because Node picks the first condition that matches, in the order the keys are written, and stops. A broad key listed first hides everything after it.

"exports": {
  ".": { "default": "./a.js",
         "import": "./a.mjs" }   // never reached
}

Here default matches first for every importer, so the ESM build is never used. Put specific conditions (types, import, require) first and default last.

code.title: Measuring event-loop delay and utilization

followUps:
CPU % says how busy the whole machine is, while ELU (event-loop utilization) says how much of the time the single JS thread was busy, from 0 to 1. A Node process can be at 100% ELU and only 12% CPU on an 8-core machine, since the other cores sit idle.

That is why the average CPU of 35% hides the problem: one thread running flat out looks small when averaged across cores. Read ELU with performance.eventLoopUtilization(); sustained values above about 0.8 mean requests queue.

Avoid vulnerable patterns, bound the input, and move risky matching off the main thread. ReDoS comes from nested or overlapping quantifiers like (a+)+$, where 30 characters can take billions of steps.

  1. Limit input length (for example 1,000 chars) before matching.
  2. Rewrite with unambiguous patterns, or use a linear-time engine such as RE2.
  3. Run untrusted patterns in a worker with a timeout, and lint patterns with a tool like safe-regex.

code.title: Unbounded cache leak vs bounded cache

followUps:
Writing a snapshot has to walk the whole heap and build a copy of its graph in memory, and V8 pauses JavaScript while it does. A 1.5 GB heap can need roughly as much again, so a process near its limit may run out of memory.

It also freezes the process for seconds, long enough for health checks to fail and the orchestrator to kill it. That is why you take snapshots on an instance drained from the load balancer, with spare memory.

It tells you that more than 10 listeners (the default) were added for one event on the same emitter, which almost always means listeners are added repeatedly and never removed.

Typical cause: calling socket.on('data', ...) inside a per-request handler on a long-lived socket. Each request adds one more listener, and each listener keeps its closure alive. The warning shows the event name and emitter; fix the registration, rather than raising the limit with setMaxListeners.

code.title: Ref'd vs unref'd timers keep the process alive

followUps:
unref() marks a timer or handle so that it no longer counts as a reason to keep the loop alive. It still fires if the process is running for other reasons.

Example: a metrics setInterval every 10 s with unref(). If the server closes and nothing else is pending, Node exits at once instead of waiting for the next tick. ref() reverses it. It does not cancel anything; use clearInterval for that.

On SIGTERM, stop taking new work, wait for in-flight work with a deadline, close resources, then exit.

process.on('SIGTERM', async () => {
  server.close();           // stop new connections
  await db.end();           // release the pool
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 10000).unref();
});

The unref'd timer is a safety net, so a stuck request cannot block shutdown forever. Make the deadline shorter than the orchestrator's kill grace period (30 s in Kubernetes by default).

Always verify claims about ordering, defaults and versions by running them on your Node version, since these are exactly where models are confidently wrong.

  • The order of nextTick, promises, setTimeout and setImmediate, in both CJS and ESM.
  • Default values such as highWaterMark and the pool size.
  • Which operations use the thread pool.
  • Whether require() of ESM works.

A one-minute experiment beats a paragraph of explanation.

Block the loop on purpose in a test and assert that your lag metric notices, and that a normal run stays below a threshold.

  1. Start monitorEventLoopDelay() and run the code path under a realistic load.
  2. Fail the test if p99 exceeds a budget, say 50 ms.
  3. Add a control case that runs a 200 ms synchronous loop and expects p99 above 150 ms, proving the monitor works.

Use generous thresholds in CI, since shared runners are noisy.
